tier_reason: README section 'Benchmark: blitsort vs std::stable_sort vs gfx::timsort' has a data table with all quoted averages (64-bit random 0.006207 vs 0.002518, 32-bit random 0.006025 vs 0.002341, descending 0.000921 vs 0.000055), states compiler and flags (WSL 2 gcc 7.5.0, g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive bench.c) and uses the public wolfsort harness, but no CPU model is given, so it is C, not A.

corrections.caveats: No CPU model is stated (only WSL 2/gcc 7.5.0), and the run is inside WSL rather than bare metal, so it falls short of tier A. The benchmark uses an old libstdc++ (gcc 7.5) and may not match current blitsort or current libstdc++. The biggest speedups are on already-ordered or patterned data, which favors adaptive sorts. On the same table blitsort is not faster everywhere: on 128-bit random order the averages are 0.011047s (std::stable_sort) vs 0.011423s (blitsort), and blitsort is slower on 'ascending tiles' (0.000948 vs 0.001397) and 'bit reversal' (0.001355 vs 0.002160). The Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant.

notes: All claimed numbers match the README table rows exactly, and the metadata checks out (Unlicense, 715 stars, last commit 2024-07-27, not a fork or archived). I only expanded the caveats to cover the 128-bit parity and the distributions where blitsort loses.

tier_reason: The checked-in results file compares Voracious against Rust sort_unstable, Rust stable sort and Rayon on i64 at 100 to 10M elements, with the CPU stated (Ryzen 3950x in computer_spec). The baseline is Rust's own sort, not C++ std::sort, and the build flags for the run are not stated, so it is first-party tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: i64 uniform, 1,000 elements: Rust std stable sort ~36us (36.80 ns/item) vs Voracious trait sort ~23us (23.57 ns/item), ~1.56x (derived from page data). At this size Voracious ties Rust sort_unstable (23.64 ns/item) because it falls back to pdqsort. The radix advantage shows at large sizes: at 1,000,000 elements single-thread Voracious takes 9311us vs Rust sort_unstable 37945us (~4.1x) and Rust stable sort 66765us (~7.2x); at 10,000,000 elements 117667us vs 535417us (~4.6x) and 757896us (~6.4x) (derived from page data). Page columns are mean time in us, standard deviation in ns and time per item in ns.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README 'Version' section lists rustc 1.46.0 stable as last tested. The results file is output from a cargo test run; the repo's .env exports RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" and the Makefile test target uses cargo test --release, but the exact invocation for this run is not stated.
corrections.caveats: This compares against Rust's own slice::sort/sort_unstable (the pdqsort-era implementations), not C++ std::sort, so compared_against_cpp_std_directly=false. Rust replaced these with driftsort/ipnsort in 1.81, so the baseline is outdated. Build flags for the run are not stated, which caps it at tier C. Below a few hundred to thousand elements Voracious falls back to Rust's pdqsort, so small-array 'wins' are only against the stable sort; the real radix gains (4-7x vs Rust sorts) appear at 1M+ elements. The trait sort may use up to 2x memory (out of place).

notes: The record's '36.525us vs 23.334us' misreads the columns: '36us 525ns' is mean 36us plus a 525ns standard deviation per the README legend. The ratio happened to come out the same, but I corrected claimed_speedup and added the representative large-array numbers. Metadata verified: MIT, 75 stars, last commit 2025-12-08, active.

tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench.sh + benchmarks/bench.c, with competitor sources vendored). The README states the GCC versions per machine, -O3 (+ -flto for the competitors), and the CPU models. The per-machine tables list geomeans matching the claim (M4: xxHash3 0.79, City 0.38, SipHash24 0.21; Power10: xxHash3 0.93, City 0.48).

corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9900X, Intel i5-13600K (the README prose says 'i5-1300K'), Intel Core Ultra 9 285 (table only), IBM Power10, Apple M4 10-core Mac mini
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1 (AMD Ryzen 9900X and Apple M4), GCC 12.3.1 (Intel), GCC 11.5.0 (IBM Power10); -O3 for all. benchmarks/bench.sh also appends -march=native on x86_64 and -mcpu=native on ppc64, and adds -flto only for the competing hash functions (not MUM/VMUM) to allow cross-file inlining. Each test is run 3x pinned with taskset -c 0 and the minimum user time is kept.
corrections.caveats: There is no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no SPDX license, but every source header (mum.h, vmum.h, mum512.h, mum-prng.h) carries the MIT permission notice. The benchmark is first-party (author's repo) but fully disclosed. xxHash3 is not beaten everywhere: it is faster than VMUM-V2 on mid-size keys (about 32/64-128 bytes, and 16 bytes on Power10; e.g. 128 bytes: 1.98x on AMD, 1.81x on M4, 2.03x on Power10) and on bulk on AMD/M4. VMUM-V1 is itself ~1.1x faster than VMUM-V2 on geomean. Timings are whole-program user time, including key generation.

notes: The claimed ratios match the M4 and Power10 geomean rows. The license is MIT via per-file headers, not unlicensed, so usability changes from reference to copyable. The tables cover 5 machines, including an Intel Ultra 9 285 not mentioned in the prose. Metadata verified: 165 stars, last commit 2026-06-02, not a fork or archived.
